title: Staton v. Boeing Co.
lead: Boeing’s discrimination settlement survived challenges to its class structure but failed scrutiny of fees and unusually large payments to a selected group.

actors.name: Class counsel
actors.role: Negotiators selecting preferred monetary recipients and a fixed fee

actors.name: Objecting class members
actors.role: Appellants challenging certification and settlement fairness

proceedings: District court: certified class and approved consent decree September 1999 after discovery into collusion and two hearings.
Ninth Circuit: upheld Rule 23(a) discretion but reversed settlement approval 2–1 and remanded.
limits: This is the substituted April 29, 2003 opinion; the November 2002 majority was withdrawn. The decision does not categorically ban incentive awards or find Boeing liable for discrimination.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Employees allege discrimination across a broad workforce
sections.cue: Introduce the claims and the negotiated exchange.
paragraphs: In 1998, African-American Boeing employees brought a class action alleging discrimination in promotion, pay, career development, and working conditions. Thirty-two named plaintiffs sought Title VII, § 1981, and other relief for about 15,000 employees in twenty-seven states, including hourly and salaried workers, supervisors and nonsupervisors, and workers from acquired businesses.

Counsel interviewed more than 1,300 employees and documented over 200 experiences across categories and locations. Formal discovery remained limited when negotiations began in November 1998. The parties announced an agreement in January 1999.

The proposed decree offered $7.3 million before reversions and opt-out adjustments, with about $6.5 million actually payable. A counsel-selected group initially numbering 264 named plaintiffs and other participants, reduced to 237 after opt-outs, would receive over half the nominal monetary relief. Individual awards ran from $5,000 to $50,000, averaging about $16,500. Roughly 3,400 other claimants averaged about $1,000 under a points system. Many selected recipients had signed individual retainers and contributed to counsel’s expenses.

sections.title: Fees and prospective terms accompany the damages allocation
sections.cue: Trace the district court’s approval and the separate certification question.
paragraphs: Boeing also agreed to about $4.05 million in fees and costs, including $200,000 for objectors’ lawyers, plus notice and expenditures attributed to prospective relief. Consultations, monitoring, and employment initiatives often left adoption to Boeing; some programs already existed. The decree generally could not enforce individual discrimination relief, and its release extended to certain contract and tort claims beyond race discrimination. Monetary members could opt out, but equitable-class members could not.

Objectors challenged certification, distribution, fees, notice, discovery, and prospective relief. After limited collusion discovery and two fairness hearings, the district court found no direct collusion, emphasized compromise and litigation risks, and approved the decree in September 1999.

Judge Berzon, joined by Judge Lay sitting by designation, found no abuse of Rule 23(a) certification discretion. Numerosity was undisputed; company-wide allegations, extensive interviews, and representative breadth supported commonality and typicality. Mixing supervisors, locations, unions, or acquired businesses was not categorically forbidden. The court acknowledged possible trial difficulties and distinguished unfair settlement allocation from proof that workforce categories inherently required separate classes. Certification was not a discrimination finding.

sections.title: Absence of collusion does not establish settlement fairness
sections.cue: Explain the fee-method problem and valuation limits.
paragraphs: Rule 23(e) independently required a fair, adequate, reasonable agreement. Even without a secret bargain, incentives could favor counsel and selected participants over absent members. Broad releases and largely consultative relief intensified scrutiny, though those concerns alone did not justify reversal.

Separate payment of fees did not remove class interests. Boeing negotiated the whole package; excess fees could still displace relief. Title VII and § 1981 allowed statutory fee shifting, reviewable through reasonable hours and rates and proper lodestar adjustments. Yet the parties supplied insufficient billing support. They instead combined damages, fees, notice, and an estimated value for prospective relief as a supposed fund and called the fee about twenty-eight percent.

The majority permitted either statutory-fee or common-fund methods with their safeguards. Ordinarily, a total fund could be agreed first and fees judicially allocated from it, or negotiated statutory fees could be justified under statutory standards. Here the fixed fee was indispensable to settlement but defended as a fund percentage, restricting meaningful control over the class-counsel division. These were paradigms, not exclusive procedures; variants with equivalent safeguards, including carefully supervised simultaneous bargaining, could work.

Speculative, undifferentiated prospective benefits could not ordinarily inflate the denominator. Consultation or monitoring expense, including already planned spending, was not necessarily measurable value to members. Removing the $3.65 million estimate raised fees to about thirty-eight percent, above the circuit’s twenty-five-percent benchmark, which was not an absolute maximum. Unusually measurable injunctive benefits might count; otherwise they could inform a percentage, lodestar, or cross-check. Reasonable notice expense could count, but duplication caused by defective initial notice should not.

sections.title: The preferred group’s much higher awards need individualized support
sections.cue: State what reasonable incentive compensation remains possible.
paragraphs: An approximately sixteenfold average payment gap lacked adequate direct support. General assertions that people who came forward must have stronger claims did not explain particular awards. Preferred nonrepresentatives also benefited, apparently sometimes because of financial relationships with counsel. Cordell Bolder, one recipient, was acknowledged not to belong to the class.

Reasonable representative incentives remained permissible with scrutiny of actions, class benefit, time, effort, and reasonable retaliation concerns. Substantiated services or expenses could be reimbursed, and credible actual or possible retaliation could justify differences. But a broad favored group could not receive unsupported damages simply for helping counsel or taking risks common to participation. A clearly nonmember’s damages payment had to be removed, although genuinely disputed membership could be compromised.

Knowledgeable participants normally helped assess class-wide fairness. Unexplained special payments could instead induce them to maximize their own recoveries. The majority required justification, not a categorical ban on all additional compensation.

sections.title: Trott would defer to the investigated compromise, but approval is reversed
sections.cue: End with remand options and the limits on judicial rewriting.
paragraphs: Judge Trott dissented. He stressed deferential review, the district court’s no-collusion finding, litigation risk, opt-outs, counsel’s explanations, and expert support. He considered prospective legal assistance and employment initiatives valuable and fees a separate component that did not diminish class relief. The disagreement concerned practical value and safeguards even absent direct misconduct.

The majority reversed approval and remanded. The parties could substantiate the distribution and justify fixed fees under statutory lodestar principles, or renegotiate and use proper common-fund procedures. The court could not unilaterally impose changed terms on a settlement that had to stand or fall as a whole. Rule 23(a) certification discretion survived, but no merits liability judgment against Boeing was entered.

The accompanying April 29, 2003 order withdrew the November 26, 2002 majority and denied rehearing and rehearing en banc. This substituted opinion, rather than the withdrawn version or the distinct later Johnson incentive-award rule mentioned in the casebook, supplies this result.

sources.pinpoint: 327 F.3d at 964 n.16, 978 n.28, 979–986; substituted-opinion order
